claims.text: Local surface composition controls the premelting and melting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Sub-surface enrichment in high-surface-energy elements raises the surface dissolution barrier.
Sub-surface enrichment in high-surface-energy elements raises the barrier to thermal atomic mobility at the surface.
A raised surface mobility barrier delays the onset of premelting.
The proposed initial material is a homogeneous, solid-solution HEA nanoparticle, exemplified by an FCC particle containing noble and high-surface-energy elements.
The controlled comparison should differ only in whether a high-surface-energy element is enriched in the sub-surface region.
Ru is an example of a high-surface-energy element.
Ru can increase the dissolution potential of neighboring Pt atoms and slightly improve the dissolution stability of Pt-Ru particles.
Incorporating an element with high relative surface energy is an alloying strategy that can stabilize nanoparticles against dissolution.
A Pd shell with sub-surface Ru can act as a passivation layer that increases nanoparticle stability against dissolution.
An individual surface atom's dissolution potential depends on its local atomic environment.
Sub-surface enrichment increases local atomic coordination-energy barriers.
Increasing local coordination-energy barriers stabilizes the surface under heating and raises the melting-onset temperature.
Enriched nanoparticles should begin surface disordering at a higher temperature than homogeneous controls.
Enriched nanoparticles should undergo complete melting at a higher temperature than homogeneous controls.
The proposed relationship should hold for compositionally comparable HEA nanoparticles with similar crystal structures, such as FCC solid solutions containing noble and higher-surface-energy metals.
The proposed relationship may fail in non-solid-solution phases, after drastic phase changes, or when segregation is uncontrolled.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in premelting and melting onset temperatures, or observation of an earlier transition, would falsify the hypothesis.
